title: A Tale of Two Movie Experiences

commenti.body:
Personally, I really enjoyed Killers and I’m ready for a rewatch. Scorsese really is a treasure to cinema. The best praise I can give to this movie is that it’s almost 4 hours long but it feels like a 150 minute movie. The cast is stellar, the ending fantastic. I really think it will grow to be considered among the master’s best. And that is saying a lot. Tbh everything he has done *after* Shutter Island has been gold.

Oppenheimer, on the other hand, was just… okay? It felt long, it was a little difficult to follow. I thought the middle portion of the movie gets good, but then everything after the Trinity Test just goes back to being *another* political thriller. I didn’t think the movie had any deep ideas or interesting themes besides the occasional “what have I done” look from Cillian Murphy. Very impressive (and packed) cast but the performances were all okay. I truly do not get the hype for RDJ’s performance here. I do gotta say, the sound design on the Trinity Test scene was very impressive.

I honestly consider both of them to be among the best films of the century so far and we are lucky to have each. I own Oppenheimer on 4k and have been studying it and am of the mind that it's not just a meme that Nolan was the perfect person to make this film, it actually vindicates his 'quantum approach' to filmmaking in many ways. What better way to tell the story of this man than through a quantum lens, interspersing the past, present and future of the important moment of his achievement in a way that allows the themes of his life to reveal themselves almost topographically, challenging us to consider that quantum science IS how reality functions and hints at a way of existing that is deeper than the soil - which, when you think of it, furthers Oppenheimer's work. Maybe that sounds grandiose but think about it. I'm not sure if I know how to put into words how I relate to it, but there's something about how the different beats of the story lower into place and sit perfectly comfortably without the constraints of linearity really impeding their coherence or in the long run seeming anything but highly yet naturally organized. I think it will only get better with each watch, personally, as by my third viewing I had realized that my misgivings with the film were shortsighted. That's my experience of course, but at the very least I will say it could be the best looking biopic ever made, and that's worth something too.

Killer Moon, however, just seems so important on both the visceral, immediate level and in the sense that it has been a long, long, long time coming. I have indigenous heritage myself, and I feel somewhat in reverence of the film. I feel so grateful for this elaborate illustration of typical shitheaded evil that I've never quite been able to put into words, I feel so grateful for Lily Gladstone's triumphant unearthing of a true to life indigenous Hero whose brave actions influenced America nearly anonymously for a century, I feel grateful for the film's insistence that who the FBI serves are more important than the FBI, I feel grateful for Scorcese's refusal to cut the story shorter, to insist that this is important to tell at exactly the length it needs to be told, to end the film with an expose that blatantly exposes the auditory whiteface that broadcasters were able to use to spin the character of Americans into an oblivious or complicit stature. It is daring, it is here and now, it is essential because this is native land and the people who want to create a white "Christian" state out of it are acting RIGHT NOW, and against all odds this aging Catholic with a rare case of honorable accountability has exposed their ways of thinking and acting for us to consider. And that isn't even scratching the surface of what the creative process of this film entailed and represent, the communal interaction and collaboration to tell a story that is not only respectful but USEFUL. And I don't mean to insult your friend but... as someone of indigenous heritage who has had to mitigate the realities of a genocidal inheritence, when I hear people are disappointed in the film I can't help but feel like they haven't spent enough time thinking about indigenous issues at all. It is a monumental film, it is, if you don't mind me saying, totemic. I envy the actors, because this is what acting is for, and there's not a performance in this where I don't see them understand it.

To me when you really break down what they are about at the root it's tough to compare the importance of the two films, but Killer Moon seems more urgent to me. The lessons we learn from Oppenheimer arguably might have the time for us to come around to, if we as a society don't decide to go flatearth before then. And funny enough, all the best of movie lists I've been reading are pointing to a plethora of profound films to consider... I almost feel like by thinking Killer Moon and Oppenheimer are the best of the year I'm going to be lumped into some kind of boy's club or typified as a predictable, mainstream movie goer, but I can't help but see the quality in these exceptional pieces. I'm going to cherish them both... they better release Killer Moon in 4k though ffs

>Maybe it's better if I read the biography American Prometheus, then I could appreciate the movie 

As a fan of the biography I found it even more disappointing how the film pivoted on the passive humiliation of Oppie's security hearing while blazing through the rest of his life and career and relationships that made him such a distinguished figure in the first place, consequently reducing the potential impact of that hearing. The portrayal of his contribution as director of perhaps the greatest team of geniuses in the history of the world is barely a token effort, and twisting an already complicated series of events into an arbitrarily non-linear structure only hampered any potential build-up.

>Oppenheimer, I feel, was too fast, that it didn't give me any time to connect with anything. It did keep the movie engaging the first time, but after I knew the plot, I guess I just wanted to know the characters better, which the movie didn't allow.

I feel this way about almost every Nolan movie. I love them the first time, and then the magic fades away after thinking about it or rewatching it. It's not necessarily a bad thing. 99% of movies don't make me love them the first time I watch them. But it keeps his movies from being some of my all-time favorites, because they get worse every time I watch them.

Even the works before Shutter Island are gold, particularly Taxi Driver, Goodfellas. But I get what you're trying to say. Scorsese has become more introspective beginning with Silence. I initially thought age has made him mellow, but his recent films just grow over me with time, even more so than the earlier works.

As for Oppenheimer, I still do like it, particularly the non-linear storytelling and the performances, but I do wish that it was just a little more slower. The Prestige had a good pace, allowing us to soak in the period setting, and notice the details that are missed on the initial viewing. It's just that after the Dark Knight Trilogy, Nolan has become a bit self-indulgent, and his flaws become more pronounced as his vision grows. Dunkirk is an exception. I still admire him for his technical mastery though, and besides Scorsese, he is one of the only few telling meaningful stories on a grand scale. 

All this said, both are decade defining movies, or even a century, as time will tell. I hope both of them sweep the Oscars, with KotFM winning Best Picture and Nolan getting Best Director. The only reason I want Nolan to win Best Director is because Scorsese has already won it.

Frankly, even I found Flower Moon weird during the first 45 minutes. I mean, I was expecting a crime drama like Goodfellas. But somewhere around the point where Chief Bonnicastle narrates the plight of the Osage and how it's difficult to identify the wolves in the modern age, that's when it hit me what Scorsese is saying with this film. After that, I got more comfortable with the deliberate pacing. Granted, I was still confused by some odd editing choices, like the juxtaposition of Anna's death, Mollie and John's voiceovers, and the radio show ending. I knew that there's a symbolism, but couldn't quite pin it the first time. This explains why I enjoyed the second viewing more than the first, since i could now appreciate the finer details, and I will definitely revisit it more often, and it has motivated me to read the book, and learn more about Osage and other indigenous culture.

Oppenheimer on the other hand, I believe is Nolan's most personal work yet. I love how the non-linear storytelling puts us right into Oppenheimer's head. I felt the cinematography was sterile the first time around, but given how the central characters are scientists, it does make sense, like this is how they see the world. 

Also kudos to Nolan for telling a biopic on such a large scale. It does suck you into the relevance of how physics shapes the contemporary world, and that's one thing we should be grateful to Nolan for. 

Finally, it is disheartening that Killers of the Flower Moon couldn't make it big at the box office, but it will be remembered for generations, open up a lot of more discussions, and encourage more filmmakers to tell such important stories on a bigger scale
Agree with the miniseries idea. In fact, I'd love to see an anthology based on everyone involved in the Manhattan project

Yeah, Killers of the Flower Moon blew me away, can’t wait to watch it again.

Oppenheimer was good, but…god it has a lot of issues that everyone seems to be ignoring. The constant Willynilly changing of aspect ratios drove me fucking nuts. 

And Nolan just can’t help himself from always inserting a “Constantly Ask Questions So Audience Gets Fed Exposition” character. With Inception me and my wife made a drinking game where we took a shot every time Elliot Page asks a character a question (we’re always hammered halfway through) and here it was Alden in the RDJ court martial timeline. Take a shot every time he asks RDJ a question, just so we can hear him explain to us something the plot needs to move forward. Again, you’ll be sloshed by the 90 min mark.

I hate to say it…but if Oppenheimer was directed by someone other than Nolan, I actually would’ve liked it more. It would’ve made 800 million less, but whatever.

I think they're both almost entirely male movies from over the hill directors with overly used actors. Both movies had opportunities to reveal truths and chose not to. The Trinity test in New Mexico resulted in infant deaths, cancer and decades of health problems for thousands. It was portrayed in the movie, however, as if it were an uninhabited barren land. Why?  Why not portray the truth?  Who would have been harmed by showing the damage that was inflicted on innocent people in the name of science?  The movie's failure to portray the real impact of that is something I don't understand. It's posturing as if it's revealing truth, but it isn't. It's white washing, making Oppenheimer into a hero. Why not a more nuanced and accurate depiction?  Because these old white men directors aren't trying to show us anything new. Maybe they're afraid that we as an audience don't want to see anything other than white male hero movies. I think they're out of touch and they can't see things through fresh eyes anymore. 

Flowers of The Killer Moon, was just another Scorcese vehicle to show us the same male actors we've been watching for decades. They're not at their best: Scorcese included. Why not tell the story from the perspective of the Osage who were actually harmed?  Lily Gladstone was fine but the film didn't even bother to translate half of the things she said when she spoke in her native tongue. She spent most of the movie moaning in bed. Here's this epic story of men harming an Indian population but we're going to use all white men to do it and to have them tell the story. Why? 

We fall all over ourselves to praise these filmmakers who aren't actually showing us anything new. Same old, same old.
That's true, but at least they've shown how to make a culturally relevant film on a large scale. Hopefully, we get more sensitive and bolder filmmakers unafraid to show something new

I would need a rewatch of Killers, but this feels accurate.

Killers was discernibly top tier cinema from a master still at the height of his craft. There was deep intention behind every nuance and detail leading to a vivid and emotional rhythmic experience. It was more restrained than expected but I feel, sort of like No Country for Old Men, it will get better with age and every re-watch.

As for Oppenheimer, it is still my favourite movie of the year, but upon a second watch you begin to see the little 'Nolanisms" pop up. Don't get me wrong, he is a master at epic grandiose filmmaking. His films are deeply cinematic and it almost brings me to tears how much this man obviously loves the craft, it bleeds through all of his work and we are blessed to have Nolan films as an experience.  


So, the 'Nolanisms'. Which are moments where I notice his decision making. Little things begin to irk me, firstly is casting. Dane DeHaan and Casey Affleck were miscasts (love them both), and to me a little bit baffling as choices. Dane looks 14 years old and after Casey's character was described with this ruthless nature, I could not make the connection once he appeared on screen. He did not fit. Nolan enjoys the set up - punchline moments a little too often. Like Emily Blunt's testimony starts very weak and then she comes around and crushes. The whole RDJ mentioning Einstein's snub throughout the film *felt like* it was all there just to deliver the "maybe it was something bigger than you" line.   


That said, I loved all of it. Including those moments, but it does eventually pull the film down a tier in terms of master craftsmanship. I want to see a story unfold effortlessly where the directors decision making doesn't pop up here and there. Scorsese achieved that more with Killers than Nolan did with Oppenheimer.

Haven't watched Killers yet, I didnt care for the Irishman and not sure I want to give Scorsese another 4 hours, but Oppenheimer moves nicely for me, but i'm mainly just counting down the minutes until Emily Blunt gets her turn in the chair.

I thought Killers of the Flower Moon was a bit arrogant. I don’t wanna see Jack White in my films for the sake of having Jack White in the cast. It’s obnoxious. I live in Nashville and the rock star-worship  here is so man-loving and so annoying. It’s such a boys’ club. Too much of that in KOTFM for me, personally.
